transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose I’m here because my doctor was… fairly insistent that I come talk to someone. She thinks my meal planning has gotten too tight, I think that was her phrase, or close to it. To me it doesn’t feel especially alarming, it feels more like keeping things orderly and not having food decisions take over the day.

I usually keep breakfast simple, like yogurt, because then I know what I’m doing and I can just get on with things. And if I’m busy, I may skip lunch—not dramatically, just because I’m working or occupied and it seems easier. Then dinner is very measured, I guess you could say. I plan it carefully so the day stays balanced and predictable. My doctor seems concerned about that pattern, so… that’s what brings me in, more than anything.
Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't follow your planned meal schedule?

I wouldn’t say “upset” exactly, at least not in a dramatic way. It’s more that I like the day to have a structure, and food is one of those areas where if I decide ahead of time, then it doesn’t take up so much space in my mind.

So, for example, breakfast is usually just yogurt because it’s simple and I know what it is. If I’m busy, lunch might just not happen, and that feels practical to me rather than concerning. And then dinner I keep very measured, because by then I want the day to feel sort of balanced and orderly. My doctor seems to think that’s too tight, and maybe that’s why she wanted me here, but from my point of view it feels more like keeping things predictable than being anxious, if that makes sense.
Do you spend a lot of time thinking about food throughout the day?

I suppose I do think about it, but maybe not in the way people mean when they ask that. It’s not that I’m sitting there daydreaming about food all day, exactly. It’s more that I like having it already decided, because then I don’t have to keep revisiting it.

So breakfast is usually yogurt, because that’s straightforward and there’s no debate. If I’m working or caught up in something, lunch can sort of fall away, and I don’t always see the point of interrupting everything for it if I’m not focused on it. Then dinner is where I’m more careful, I guess—I make it very measured so the day feels orderly and balanced.

My doctor seems to think that level of planning has gotten too tight, and maybe that’s why she’s concerned. But to me, it feels less like obsessing and more like keeping things contained so food doesn’t become this big, messy decision every few hours.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight recently?

Yes… I mean, I suppose there has been some change. My weight has gone down, not in what I would have called a dramatic way, but enough that my doctor clearly noticed it and didn’t like the direction of it.

When she showed me the chart, I could see what she meant—there’s a downward drift. But I also have this reaction where I look at the number and think, well, if it were just a little lower, it would feel cleaner somehow. More manageable. Like a tidier number to keep track of. I know that probably sounds odd when I say it out loud, but that’s the thought I have.

So yes, it has gone down more than my doctor is comfortable with. I’m not sure I feel the same level of concern about it, though.
Do you have any fear of gaining weight?

Yes… I think that’s probably the honest answer, even though I don’t like the word “fear” because it makes it sound so irrational or childish. But if I get on the scale and it’s up even a pound—like after a perfectly normal dinner, or if I’ve gone out to a restaurant and eaten something I didn’t measure myself—I feel this very sharp panic.

It’s not just, “Oh, that’s annoying.” It feels like I’ve lost control of the situation somehow, like the number is moving away from me and I need to pull it back quickly. And then I start thinking about the next day, what I should do to correct it, how to make things feel even again. I know logically a pound can be all sorts of things, but in the moment it doesn’t feel logical. It feels like I’ve done something wrong and have to fix it.
Does the feeling of panic when you gain weight have more to do with losing control or the actual weight gain itself?

I think it’s both, but if I’m being precise, the panic feels more about losing control. The pound itself is almost… well, I know on some level that a pound after dinner or after eating at a restaurant isn’t necessarily real weight in the way I’m treating it. I do know that. But when I see it on the scale, it doesn’t feel like a neutral fluctuation. It feels like evidence that I let something get away from me.

Especially if I didn’t make the food myself or I couldn’t measure it properly, then the number going up feels like confirmation that I wasn’t careful enough. And then my mind goes straight to, “Okay, tomorrow has to be corrected,” or “I need to make the day more controlled again.” It’s less like I’m calmly upset about the actual amount and more like this sharp alarm that the system isn’t holding.

So yes, the weight gain bothers me, obviously, but I think the worse part is the feeling that I’ve lost control and have to pull everything back into line.
Do you think your meal planning is mostly about maintaining your current weight?

I suppose I would have said it’s about maintaining things, yes, but maybe not only weight exactly. It’s more that if I plan the meals very tightly, the day feels orderly, and I don’t have to keep making decisions.

I came in because my doctor seems concerned that it’s gotten too rigid. To me it doesn’t always look that extreme. Breakfast is usually just yogurt because it’s simple and contained, and then if I’m busy at work or running errands, lunch can sort of disappear without it feeling like a big decision. And dinner is… measured. I like knowing what’s in it and how much, so the day ends in a way that feels controlled.

So yes, part of it is probably about not gaining weight, but in my mind it’s also about keeping the day neat. If breakfast is predictable, and lunch doesn’t complicate things, and dinner is something I can account for, then I feel like I’ve stayed on track. My doctor seems to think that’s too tight, and maybe that’s why she wanted me to talk about it.
Do you think your meal planning is mostly driven by a desire to avoid being fat?

I don’t know if I would phrase it exactly as “avoiding being fat,” because that sounds so blunt and almost… cruel, somehow. But yes, there is definitely something in me that is trying very hard not to let my weight go up.

When I plan food, it feels like I’m preventing things from slipping. Like if I eat a normal dinner, or especially if I’ve been at a restaurant where I don’t really know what was in everything, and then the scale is up even a pound the next morning, I get this really sharp panic. It’s immediate. I don’t just think, “Oh, bodies fluctuate.” I think, “I’ve lost control,” and then I start thinking about what I need to do the next day to correct it.

So maybe it’s less that I’m walking around using the word “fat” in my head all day, but the fear is there. The meal planning is partly to keep that panic from happening — to keep the number from surprising me, I suppose.
Is your strict meal planning more about preventing weight gain or about feeling in control of your daily routine?

I think… it’s hard to separate them, honestly. If I had to choose, I’d say it feels more like control over the day, or keeping the day from getting messy. But of course the weight part is tangled up in that, because the reason I want the day so orderly is partly so nothing unexpected happens with my weight.

I came in because my doctor was concerned that my meal planning has gotten too tight. I don’t always see it that way in the moment. To me it feels practical, almost. Breakfast is yogurt because I know what it is, it’s simple, and I don’t have to think too much. Then if I’m busy or I’m out doing errands, lunch can sort of get skipped without it feeling like some major decision. And then dinner is the meal I really want to be measured and accounted for, so I know how the day ends.

So I suppose the honest answer is that the routine gives me a sense of control. It makes the day feel orderly. But I can also see that it’s serving the purpose of preventing weight gain, or at least preventing that panic that comes when I feel like I haven’t kept things contained.
Is the thought of gaining weight what motivates you to plan your meals so strictly?

Yes, I think it is, though I don’t always admit that to myself in those words. It’s not like I sit down with a notebook and think, “I must not gain weight,” in such a clear, dramatic way. It’s more that if I don’t plan things strictly, I feel exposed to something going wrong.

It feels like I need to do something to correct it the next day.

So yes, I suppose the thought of gaining weight is a big part of why I plan so carefully. The planning makes me feel like I can prevent that panic from happening.

So yes, preventing weight gain is probably the center of it. The planning is how I try to stop that panic from happening.
